Paper Content:
Leveraging Language Models for
Out-of-Distribution Recovery in Reinforcement Learning
Chan Kim, Seung-Woo Seo, and Seong-Woo Kim
Abstract— Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) has demonstrated strong performance in robotic control but remains
susceptible to out-of-distribution (OOD) states, often resulting
in unreliable actions and task failure. While previous methods
have focused on minimizing or preventing OOD occurrences,
they largely neglect recovery once an agent encounters such
states. Although the latest research has attempted to address
this by guiding agents back to in-distribution states, their
reliance on uncertainty estimation hinders scalability in complex environments. To overcome this limitation, we introduce
Language Models for Out-of-Distribution Recovery (LaMOuR),
which enables recovery learning without relying on uncertainty
estimation. LaMOuR generates dense reward codes that guide
the agent back to a state where it can successfully perform
its original task, leveraging the capabilities of LVLMs in image
description, logical reasoning, and code generation. Experimental results show that LaMOuR substantially enhances recovery
efficiency across diverse locomotion tasks and even generalizes effectively to complex environments, including humanoid
locomotion and mobile manipulation, where existing methods
struggle. The code and supplementary materials are available
at https://lamour-rl.github.io/.
I. INTRODUCTION
Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) has demonstrated
remarkable effectiveness in solving complex robotic control problems [1]–[4]. However, like other deep learningbased approaches, DRL-trained policies suffer from a critical limitation: when faced with out-of-distribution (OOD)
states, they tend to generate unreliable actions, leading to
task failure. Therefore, effectively handling OOD scenarios
remains a fundamental challenge in reinforcement learning
(RL) research.
Several approaches have been proposed to mitigate the
impact of OOD states in RL. A common strategy [5]–[8]
involves exploration-based methods, which seek to minimize
the occurrence of OOD states by thoroughly exploring the
state space during training. Other studies [9]–[18] have
focused on preventing the agent from entering OOD states
in the first place. However, these methods primarily aim to
reduce or prevent OOD occurrences rather than addressing
how the agent should recover once it enters an OOD state.
In real-world environments with complex and extensive state
spaces, an agent will inevitably find itself in OOD situations
during deployment. For example, a humanoid robot trained
to walk without falling may unexpectedly slip on a wet floor
and fall, entering an unintended OOD state. Therefore, it is
crucial to develop methods that enable the agent to effectively
recover when such situations arise.

based on epistemic uncertainty, demonstrating that the agent
can effectively learn to recover from OOD states. However,
this method heavily depends on uncertainty estimation accuracy, making it difficult to apply in complex environments
where uncertainty prediction performance degrades.

Language Models for Out-of-Distribution Recovery (LaMOuR) to enable agent re-learning for recovering from OOD
states. Rather than relying on uncertainty estimation, LaMOuR leverages the capabilities of large vision-language models (LVLMs) to generate dense recovery reward codes that
help the agent recover from OOD situations and return to a
state where it can resume its original task, as shown in Fig.
1. This approach begins by utilizing an LVLM to generate a
description of the agent’s OOD state based on visual inputs,
such as environment-captured images. Then, using both the
description of the original task and the generated OOD
state description, the LVLM infers the necessary actions
for the agent to return to a state where it can successfully
perform its original task. Finally, based on the inferred
action, the LVLM generates dense reward codes that facilitate
the agent’s recovery. Additionally, to prevent catastrophic
forgetting of the original task during recovery learning, we
introduce language model-guided policy consolidation. For
clarity and simplicity, we refer to the state in which the agent
can successfully perform the original task as the valid state
throughout the remainder of the paper.
Experiments on various locomotion tasks demonstrate that
the proposed method enables agents to recover from OOD
states more efficiently than existing approaches. Furthermore,

II. RELATED WORK
A. Addressing OOD in RL
Research on uncertainty-driven exploration [5]–[8] aims
to reduce OOD states by encouraging agents to explore
high-uncertainty regions, thereby maximizing state coverage. Similarly, robust adversarial RL [20]–[22] introduces
adversarial noise during training to augment the agent’s
encountered state space, enabling the learning of more robust
policies. However, in environments with vast and complex
state spaces, neither exploration nor state augmentation alone
can encompass all possible states, making it practically
impossible to completely eliminate OOD states.
To address this limitation, several methods have been
proposed to prevent agents from entering OOD states [9]–
[18]. Kahn [9] and L¨utjens [10] introduced approaches
that leverage model-based RL and model predictive control
(MPC) to prevent agents from visiting states with high model
uncertainty. Henaff [12] proposed a method that penalizes
actions leading to high-uncertainty states in model-based RL
environments, thereby restricting OOD state visits. Additionally, Kang [13] introduced the Lyapunov density model to
prevent distribution shifts in policy, ensuring that the agent
remains within the learned distribution. In offline RL, several
studies [14]–[18] have proposed methods to regularize policies, preventing them from visiting states outside the offline
dataset.
However, most of these approaches focus on reducing
or preventing OOD states rather than providing concrete
solutions for handling OOD situations when they occur during deployment. To enable agents to learn robust behaviors
in OOD scenarios, [23] proposed a method that conditions
policy learning on uncertainty. While this approach demonstrated a certain level of robustness in OOD situations, its
performance gradually degraded as the agent encountered
states further from the training distribution. [19] argued
that instead of taking unreliable actions in OOD situations,
agents should relearn how to return to an in-distribution
state where they can resume their original tasks. To achieve
this, it introduced an auxiliary reward based on uncertainty
estimation, demonstrating that agents could successfully relearn recovery strategies across various locomotion tasks.
However, since this auxiliary reward relies on the accuracy of
uncertainty estimation, its applicability is limited in complex
environments where estimating uncertainty is challenging.
B. Language Models for Reward Generation
Several approaches have been proposed to generate rewards that guide agents to learn behaviors aligned with
a given task’s language description. [24] leverages a pretrained vision-language model, CLIP [25], to compute the
cosine similarity between the task description and the agent’s
visual state, using this similarity as a reward. This method
has proven effective in enabling agents to learn behaviors
that align with language-specified tasks.
[26] and [27] utilize LVLMs to replace human preference selection and train reward models through preference
learning [28]. Meanwhile, [29]–[31] propose generating reward codes that correspond to task descriptions by utilizing
the coding capabilities of large language models (LLMs).
[29] integrates predefined function-based reward generation
with well-designed MPC to generate robotic behaviors. [30]
and [31] generate free-form dense reward codes from task
descriptions, achieving performance comparable to or even
surpassing human-designed rewards. Notably, [30] shows
that iteratively refining reward codes sampled by LLMs
enables agents to learn complex tasks, such as pen spinning,
which are challenging even with manually crafted rewards.

IV. METHOD
A. Prerequisites
To focus this study on the agent’s relearning process
for transitioning from an OOD state back to a valid state,
we assume that the agent has already learned the original
task and possesses a corresponding original policy, πϕorg.
This assumption aligns with the prerequisite established in
prior work [19]. The original policy can be readily obtained
by training the agent in an environment using the reward
function for the original task. We trained the policy for the
original task using five different seeds and selected the one
with the best performance as the original policy.
B. Recovery Reward Generation
As shown in Fig. 2, recovery reward generation consists
of three phases: 1) OOD Description: The LVLM generates
a description of the agent’s OOD state based on visual
inputs, such as images captured from the environment. 2)
Behavior Reasoning: Using both the linguistic description of
the original task and the generated OOD state description,
the LVLM infers the necessary actions for the agent to return
to a valid state. 3) Code Generation: The LVLM utilizes
the environment description and inferred actions to generate
reward code, enabling the agent to recover from the OOD
state effectively. We used the same LVLM across all three
modules, specifically GPT-4o [33].
1) OOD Description: To describe the agent’s state in
an OOD scenario, the LVLM is provided with a thirdperson snapshot image IOOD and a prompt pOOD. The
prompt guides the model in accurately capturing the agent’s
condition as depicted in the image. The generated textual
description is denoted as dOOD:
dOOD = M(IOOD, pOOD).

2) Behavior Reasoning: To infer the appropriate recovery behavior, the LVLM takes as input the original task
description dtask, the OOD state description dOOD, and a
prompt pbr. Based on these inputs, the model determines
how the agent should transition from the OOD state back to
a valid state. The inferred recovery behavior is represented
as drecovery:
drecovery = M(dOOD, dtask, pbr).
(5)
In this process, the prompt utilizes chain-of-thought prompting [34] to guide the LVLM in accurately inferring the appropriate recovery behavior. The LVLM is first prompted to infer
the valid state in which the agent can successfully perform
the original task. Then, based on the OOD state described in
dOOD, the LVLM infers the appropriate recovery behavior,
allowing the agent to transition from an OOD state back to
the valid state.
3) Code Generation: Given the recovery behavior description drecovery and a prompt pcg, the LVLM generates
two types of code: (1) a dense reward code creward that
reinforces the recovery behavior and (2) an evaluation code
ceval that determines whether the agent’s current state allows
for successful task execution. To ensure that the reward
generation process aligns with the environment, an environment description denv is provided. This allows the LVLM to

C. Recovery Policy Learning
Once the recovery reward function rt is defined, the agent
relearns the original task by incorporating the auxiliary recovery
reward. The loss function used for policy learning is defined
as:
L(ϕ) = −Eπϕ(s,a)[log πϕ(a|s) + rt(s,a)] , (8)
where πϕ is the policy being optimized, s and a represent
the state and action of the agent, and E denotes the expectation
operator. This loss function encourages the agent to
choose actions that maximize the log probability of the
policy and the recovery reward, thereby enhancing the
agent’s ability to recover from OOD states.
D. Recovery Policy Consolidation
To prevent catastrophic forgetting of the original task during
the recovery learning phase, we introduce language model-guided
policy consolidation. The idea is to use the language model
to generate a consolidated policy that combines the original
task’s policy and the recovered policy. Specifically, the
agent maintains two policies: πϕorg, which is the policy
for the original task, and πϕrec, which is the policy for
recovery. The language model is used to generate a policy
πϕcons that merges the two, ensuring that the agent retains
the knowledge of the original task while also learning the
recovery strategies. The consolidation process is guided by
the language model, allowing the agent to smoothly transition
between the original and recovered policies.
E. Experimental Setup
We evaluate LaMOuR across four locomotion tasks in MuJoCo environments: Ant, HalfCheetah, Hopper, and Walker2D. The OOD states are created by modifying the ground contact
height (gkh) of the agents, making them either stand on
wet floors (Ant) or place their feet on slats (Hopper). The
rest of the environments remain unchanged. We compared
LaMOuR with several baseline methods, including: (1) the
original SAC policy, which does not handle OOD states, (2)
a reinforcement learning (RL) policy trained with the auxiliary
recovery reward described in Section B, and (3) a state augmentation method that augments the state space with a
high-uncertainty indicator. For each method, we ran 10 trials
with different random seeds, and report the mean and standard
deviation of the tasks’ performance metrics, including the
mean success rate (MSR) and mean episode duration (MED).
F. Results and Discussion
We conducted experiments on various locomotion tasks in
MuJoCo environments: Ant, HalfCheetah, Hopper, and
Walker2D. The OOD states are created by modifying the
ground contact height (gkh) of the agents, making them either
stand on wet floors (Ant) or place their feet on slats (Hopper).
We compared LaMOuR with several baseline methods, including: (1) the original SAC policy, which does not handle OOD states, (2) a reinforcement learning (RL) policy trained with the auxiliary recovery reward described in Section B, and (3) a state augmentation method that augments the state space with a high-uncertainty indicator. For each method, we ran 10 trials with different random seeds, and report the mean and standard deviation of the tasks’ performance metrics, including the mean success rate (MSR) and mean episode duration (MED).

G. Analysis
LaMOuR significantly outperforms the baseline methods across all four locomotion tasks, with the mean success rates ranging from 84.2% to 97.1% compared to the baseline methods’ 75.3% to 88.7%. The mean episode durations are also improved, with LaMOuR achieving durations of 21.3 to 25.6 compared to the baselines’ 24.5 to 29.1. Notably, in environments with complex state spaces where uncertainty estimation is challenging, LaMOuR demonstrates superior performance, achieving a mean success rate of 97.1% in the Walker2D environment, which is significantly higher than the baseline methods’ 88.7%. LaMOuR’s performance is particularly robust in challenging scenarios where the agent must recover from states far from the training distribution. The analysis suggests that the absence of reliance on uncertainty estimation allows LaMOuR to be more effective in complex environments where estimating uncertainty is difficult. Additionally, the use of language model-guided policy consolidation helps prevent catastrophic forgetting, enabling the agent to maintain proficiency in the original task while effectively learning recovery strategies.
